summary: We demonstrate that pulsing a parametrically activated Purcell decay channel in a flux-tunable transmon qubit creates a temporal diffraction grating in the dissipation spectrum. Pulsed on/off modulation reorganizes the qubit's decay into interference fringes analogous to N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction, with each modulation window acting as a temporal aperture whose spacing, contrast, and envelope are controlled by the pulse duration and duty cycle.
motivation: Dissipation engineering in superconducting circuits traditionally relies on static spectral shaping or continuous coherent drives, but time-domain control of loss channels offers a complementary control knob for open quantum system dynamics.
method: We apply periodic on/off gating to a parametric flux modulation ($\omega_m \approx 1.308$ GHz, $g_{\mathrm{eff}}/2\pi = 0.14$ MHz) that couples a transmon ($\omega_{q,\mathrm{on}}/2\pi = 4.259$ GHz) to a readout resonator ($\omega_r/2\pi = 6.8759$ GHz, $\kappa/2\pi = 0.375$ MHz) and measure the excited-state probability as a function of modulation detuning while varying $\tau_{\mathrm{on}}$ and $\tau_{\mathrm{off}}$. We model the dynamics using a Chebyshev-polynomial propagator formalism for repeated on/off blocks.
result: Central interference dips are spaced by $\delta(\Delta_m/2\pi) = 1/(2t_c)$ where $t_c = \tau_{\mathrm{on}} + \tau_{\mathrm{off}}$ is the cycle time; the measured spectra match simulations from Eq. (3) and exhibit single-slit sinc$^2$ envelopes whose width is controlled by $\tau_{\mathrm{on}}$ while interference contrast scales with duty cycle, enabling independent tuning of fringe spacing and visibility without changing device parameters.
